author: Winsome Pinnock
year_first_performed: 1987 (Liverpool Playhouse Studio, directed by Kate Rowland)
auditor_note: Factual errors only. Interpretation and thematic emphasis not flagged. Sources: Wikipedia, RevisionWorld, Shalom Education detailed scene guide, Sierz.co.uk Bush Theatre review, Breaking the Fourth Wall Tower Theatre review, Afridiziak review, Nick Hern Books preface/blog, Critics of Colour Collective review, WhatsOnStage Bush Theatre review, Oak National Academy lesson pages (multiple), GradeSaver background, WJEC Eduqas PDF resource.

fact_base.structure: Eight scenes (not two named acts). The play is sometimes described with a loose two-part structure but the published text is organised as eight continuous scenes. Two settings: Mai's Deptford bedsit (Scenes 1, 6, 7, 8) and Enid's living room in North London (Scenes 2, 3, 4, 5).
fact_base.first_scene_setting: Mai's Deptford bedsit, Easter Monday. Enid takes Del and Viv to Mai for a reading. Del stays behind when the others leave.
fact_base.del_age_order: Del (Delores) is the ELDER daughter, age 18. Viv (Vivienne) is the YOUNGER daughter, age 17.
fact_base.del_character: Rebellious, 18 years old. Stays out late. Loses her job after arguing with her manager. Initially refuses to have her palm read by Mai. Eventually moves out of home to live with Mai. Discovers she is dyslexic. Becomes pregnant (father absent). Forms a close bond with Mai who recognises her potential as an Obeah woman. By the final scene, Del is becoming Mai's successor — Mai bequeaths her notebook to Del.
fact_base.viv_character: Younger daughter, age 17. Academically focused; preparing for A-level exams. Attempts to rebel by walking out of one of her exams. Plans to study Black Studies at university. Says 'no matter how hard I search for myself in them books, I'm never there.' Considers a gap year visit to Jamaica.
fact_base.enid_character: First-generation Jamaican immigrant. Hospital cleaner (works long hours / two jobs). Moved to England around 1959. Abandoned by her husband (the girls' father), who was abusive — he received horrific racist abuse at work which made him hard and cruel; Brod reveals this to Del in Scene 7. Feels ashamed of her poor Jamaican roots though she sends money home. Has a strained relationship with her own mother in Jamaica; her mother called her 'Miss English'. Learns of her mother's death in Scene 3. Falls into depression. Ejects Viv and Brod from home at one point. Eventually reconciles with Del.
fact_base.enids_secret: Enid's secrets/hidden past include: (1) her husband's abusive behaviour which she never told the girls; (2) her shame about her poor Jamaican roots; (3) her estrangement from her own mother; (4) a letter from her sister Cynthia in Jamaica claiming their mother is sick and requesting money — Enid suspects her sister is lying. There is NO evidence in the play text that Enid left a child behind in Jamaica. The 'abandoned child in Jamaica' is NOT Enid's secret in the play. Her mother's death — not an abandoned child — is the revelation in Scene 3.
fact_base.mai_character: Obeah woman who lives in a Deptford bedsit. Practises Caribbean folk healing/divination including palm reading. Physically declining (nearly faints at one point; dying by the end of the play). Has an estranged adult son. Becomes a maternal figure to Del. Recognises Del's potential as her successor. In the final scene (Scene 8) she gives Del her notebook and leaves Del with Enid as her first 'client'. She charges no fee for Enid's reading out of sympathy.
fact_base.brod_character: Broderick — Enid's childhood friend from Jamaica; appears on stage throughout the play (NOT an absent character). Plays a significant role in Scenes 2, 3, 7. Is the play's only significant male character. Has a serious drinking problem. Has children he no longer sees. Is disaffected about life in England. In Scene 7 he tells Del about her father's abuse of Enid and about racism. Is eventually ejected from Enid's home by her. Describes a friend (Gullyman) who suffered a breakdown despite financial success.
fact_base.final_scene: Scene 8. Del reads Enid's palm. Mai has given Del her notebook and left. Viv is going to university to read Black Studies. Del refuses to return home with Enid. Symbolically, a half-burnt white candle sits by Mai (her life/role ending) and a fully-lit candle sits in front of Del (new beginning, spiritual inheritance).
fact_base.del_palm_reading: It is DEL who reads ENID's palm in the final scene — not the other way around. This is the reconciliation moment. Mai previously read Enid's palm and predicted a 'long journey'.
fact_base.pregnancy: DEL becomes pregnant. Her pregnancy is confirmed in the play; the father is absent. Enid's original worry in Scene 1 is that Del might be pregnant — this concern is later proven correct. VIV's pregnancy is NOT a plot point in this play.
fact_base.enid_mother_death: Enid's MOTHER dies in Jamaica. Enid learns of this in Scene 3. In Scene 1 Enid tells Mai she received a letter from her sister Cynthia saying their mother is ill and requesting money; Enid suspects it may be a lie. Mai advises sending the money. The mother then dies (Scene 3), causing Enid's breakdown. This is distinct from any claim about an 'abandoned child'.
fact_base.premiere: 11 November 1987, Liverpool Playhouse Studio (directed by Kate Rowland). Subsequent major productions: Lyric Hammersmith 1990 (Hettie Macdonald); National Theatre 1994 (Gulbenkian / Cottesloe) — first play by a Black British woman produced at the National Theatre; Bush Theatre 2018 (Madani Younis). Won the George Devine Award 1991.
fact_base.play_setting_time: 1984, London — evidenced by the Easter Monday opening and 1980s context.
fact_base.title_meanings: Multiple layered meanings: Enid's departure from Jamaica; the daughters' departure from their mother's values and expectations; Mai's departure (death); Del's 'leave-taking' of her old rebellious self; the family's gradual leave-taking of shame and denial.
fact_base.brod_absent_father_confusion: The play does NOT feature an absent father as a dramatic device in the way that some study guides imply (i.e. the father does not appear on stage but is discussed). The father abandoned Enid. Brod is NOT the father — he is a family friend.

findings.lesson_title: Act 1: Enid, Viv & the Obeah Woman
findings.claim: "Viv, the elder daughter, is intelligent, ambitious and outwardly assimilated. She is preparing for university and seems to accept English culture as her own. Del, the younger daughter, is more rebellious and curious about her Caribbean roots."
findings.issue: Del is the ELDER daughter (age 18) and Viv is the YOUNGER (age 17). The lesson has the age-order of the sisters inverted. Viv is academically focused and preparing for A-level exams (not 'preparing for university' directly — she later plans to do a Black Studies degree, but at this point in the play she is studying for A-levels). Del being 'younger' is factually wrong.
findings.correction: Del is the elder daughter (18); Viv is the younger (17). Change all references accordingly. Viv is preparing for A-level exams in Act 1, not university directly.
findings.source: Shalom Education character guide (ages 18 and 17 confirmed); Sierz.co.uk Bush Theatre review ('rebellious 18-year-old daughter Del', 'studious 17-year-old daughter Viv'); Breaking the Fourth Wall review ('Del: Eldest daughter'; 'Viv: Younger daughter studying for A-levels'); multiple GCSE study sources.

findings.claim: "Second, Viv — the apparently conformist daughter — reveals that she is pregnant, demolishing the respectable future Enid has planned for her."
findings.issue: It is DEL, not Viv, who becomes pregnant. Viv's crisis in the play is walking out of an exam and wrestling with identity and education — her pregnancy is not a plot point. Attributing the pregnancy to Viv is a significant factual error that inverts two of the play's major character developments.
findings.correction: Del becomes pregnant (the father is absent). Viv's parallel crisis is her rebellion against the Euro-centric education system — she walks out of an exam and ultimately chooses to study Black Studies at university.

findings.claim: "The emotional climax of the play comes when Enid's long-buried secret is finally revealed: she left a child behind in Jamaica when she emigrated to England. This revelation reframes everything the audience has seen. Enid's obsessive desire to control her daughters' futures is not simply about ambition or snobbery — it is driven by guilt over the child she abandoned."
findings.issue: There is no evidence in the published play text that Enid left a child behind in Jamaica. This appears to be a fabricated plot point. The actual secrets/revelations in the play are: (1) Enid's mother dies in Jamaica (Scene 3) — a grief she has been anticipating through the estrangement; (2) Enid was abandoned by an abusive husband — this is revealed by Brod to Del in Scene 7; (3) Enid's shame about her poor Jamaican roots. The 'abandoned child' narrative is not documented in any reliable source as a plot event in this play.
findings.correction: Remove all references to an abandoned child in Jamaica. The key revelation is that Enid's mother has died in Jamaica (Scene 3), which triggers Enid's emotional breakdown. A second revelation (Scene 7) is that Enid's husband was physically abusive — information Brod discloses to Del. Enid's controlling behaviour stems from her experiences of racism, her husband's abandonment, and her determination to protect her daughters from the hardships she endured.
findings.source: No source confirms an 'abandoned child' plot point. The mother's death appears consistently across: Oak National Academy Scene 3 lesson title; multiple GCSE study guides referencing 'grandmother's death'; Shalom Education confirming 'Enid struggles with family dynamics and her mother's death'. Brod's revelation about the abusive father confirmed by Oak National Academy Brod character lesson and multiple GCSE guides.

findings.claim: "The emotional climax of the play comes when Enid's long-buried secret is finally revealed: she left a child behind in Jamaica when she emigrated to England."

findings.claim: "After the twin revelations of Act 2 — Viv's pregnancy and Enid's abandoned child — the family is forced to confront truths they have been avoiding for years."
findings.issue: Both 'revelations' named here are wrong. (1) It is Del, not Viv, who becomes pregnant. (2) There is no 'abandoned child' in Jamaica — this plot point does not exist in the play. The actual crises driving the Act 2 confrontation are: Del moving out of home to live with Mai; Enid's grief following her mother's death; Del's pregnancy; and Brod's revelation to Del about her father's abuse.
findings.correction: The confrontation builds from: Del leaving home and living at Mai's (a source of great distress to Enid); Enid's grief over her mother's death; Del's pregnancy; and the revelation (via Brod) of the father's abusive history. Viv's parallel arc concerns her education rebellion — she walks out of an exam and plans to study Black Studies.
findings.source: Scene structure confirmed across Oak National Academy lesson resources (Scene 3 = mother's death; Scene 6 = Enid visits Mai searching for Del; Scene 7 = Brod tells Del about father); pregnancy = Del per Shalom Education and multiple revision guides.

But Pinnock complicates this apparent conformity through Viv's pregnancy — a secret that shatters Enid's carefully constructed narrative of respectability."
findings.issue: VIV does NOT become pregnant in this play. It is DEL who becomes pregnant. Viv's 'complication' in the play is her walking out of an exam and her rejection of Eurocentric education, ultimately choosing to study Black Studies. This is a significant factual error in the character analysis.
findings.correction: Remove Viv's pregnancy entirely. Viv's rebellion is educational/intellectual — she walks out of an exam, saying the education system does not represent her experience ('no matter how hard I search for myself in them books, I'm never there'). She ultimately plans to study Black Studies at university, which is her resolution.
findings.source: Shalom Education ('Viv…Walks out of her first exam in an act of defiance. Plans to study Black Studies at university'); multiple GCSE guides confirming Del is pregnant, not Viv.

findings.claim: "Enid's guilt about her abandoned child cannot be erased."
findings.issue: There is no abandoned child. This repeats the fabricated plot point from LT-005. No reliable published source identifies an abandoned child in Jamaica as a plot point in Leave Taking.
findings.correction: Remove. Enid's unresolvable grief relates to her mother's death, her estrangement from her Jamaican past, and the damage her strategy of assimilation has caused in her relationship with her daughters.

findings.claim: "Act 2 intensifies these conflicts until they crack open: Del deepens her involvement with Obeah, Viv's pregnancy is revealed, and Enid's secret about the abandoned child emerges."
findings.issue: Two factual errors repeated: (1) Viv does not become pregnant — Del does; (2) there is no abandoned child. Additionally, the play is structured in eight scenes, not presented as two clearly demarcated 'Act 1' / 'Act 2' divisions in the published text (though a loose structural two-part reading is sometimes applied). The lesson should not describe a 'two-act structure' as if each act has a formal break and title.
findings.correction: Del's pregnancy is a key crisis. Enid's secret concerns her shame about her poor Jamaican roots, the abusive marriage she left, and her estrangement from her own mother (who dies in Scene 3). The play has eight scenes, with a structural shift roughly in the middle — but it is not divided into two formally named acts.
findings.source: Eight-scene structure confirmed: Oak National Academy lesson series (Scene 1 through Scene 8 each have dedicated lesson pages); WJEC Eduqas PDF resource; multiple revision guides referencing specific scene numbers.

findings.correction: Remove the abandoned-child framing. Enid's grief and protectiveness can be accurately explained by: her mother's death in Jamaica (Scene 3); her abusive marriage; her experience of racism as a Windrush immigrant; and her shame about her poor Jamaican roots.

findings.lesson_title: Act 1: Enid, Viv & the Obeah Woman
findings.claim: "Act 1 hints at a secret in Enid's past — something connected to Jamaica that she has never told her daughters."
findings.issue: The framing of 'a secret' as a single mystery being withheld is an oversimplification and will reinforce the fabricated 'abandoned child' narrative developed in later lessons. In Act 1 (Scene 1) the concrete concern Enid raises with Mai is: (a) a letter from her sister Cynthia saying their mother is ill and asking for money — Enid suspects this is a lie; and (b) worry that Del may be pregnant. These are Enid's specific disclosed worries in Scene 1, not a dramatised single 'hidden secret'. The deeper secrets (the abusive marriage, the estrangement from her mother) unfold across subsequent scenes.
findings.correction: In Scene 1, Enid tells Mai about the letter from her sister in Jamaica regarding their ill mother, and her worry about Del's behaviour. The sense of unspoken history is built gradually. The 'secret' framing should not be used in a way that primes students for a single dramatic revelation that does not occur.
findings.source: WJEC Eduqas PDF resource (Scene 1 summary); Oak National Academy Scene 1 page; Shalom Education character guide.

findings.claim: The lesson implies the play is set only in 'Enid's home in London', treating it as a single domestic setting.
findings.issue: The play has TWO settings: (1) Mai's Deptford bedsit (Scenes 1, 6, 7, 8 — the opening and closing scenes take place here); (2) Enid's North London living room (Scenes 2–5). The lesson's reference to the 'domestic setting' and 'Enid's home' is accurate for part of the play but omits Mai's bedsit as a distinct, equally important setting. The play begins and ends at Mai's, which is structurally significant.
findings.correction: The play has two settings: Enid's living room and Mai's Deptford bedsit. The play opens and closes at Mai's bedsit, which is symbolically important — the spiritual/Caribbean space bookends the domestic/English space.
findings.source: Sierz.co.uk review; WJEC Eduqas PDF resource (Scene 1 setting confirmed as Mai's Deptford bedsit); Breaking the Fourth Wall review; multiple GCSE guides.

findings.correction: Remove the abandoned child claim. Enid's backstory that she shares/reveals includes: her abusive marriage (husband eventually abandons her after domestic violence); her shame about her poor Jamaican roots; her estrangement from her mother in Jamaica. Her controlling behaviour is driven by her determination to protect her daughters from racism and poverty, not guilt over an abandoned child.

findings.claim: "Leave Taking is set in 1980s London — a city where Caribbean communities had established themselves but still faced racism and social marginalisation. The domestic setting (Enid's home) is crucial..."
findings.issue: The play has two physical settings: Enid's North London living room AND Mai's Deptford bedsit. Stating that 'the domestic setting (Enid's home) is crucial' without mentioning Mai's bedsit understates the spatial structure. The play opens and closes at Mai's bedsit — a fact with thematic significance (the spiritual/Caribbean space frames the whole narrative). Additionally the play's time is more precisely 1984 (Easter Monday opening), which contextualises the Thatcher-era backdrop more accurately than just '1980s'.
findings.correction: Note both settings: Enid's North London living room and Mai's Deptford bedsit. The play opens at Mai's (Scene 1) and closes there (Scene 8), with scenes 2–5 at Enid's home. The more precise date is 1984.
findings.source: WJEC Eduqas PDF (Scene 1: 'Easter Monday, 1984, Mai's bedsit'); multiple reviews confirming Deptford bedsit setting.

findings.claim: "Leave Taking is divided into two acts."
findings.issue: The published text of Leave Taking is organised into eight scenes, not two formally titled acts. While some productions and some study guides apply a loose two-part structural reading (the first half building tension, the second half exploding it), the play does not have formally numbered or titled 'Act 1' and 'Act 2' in the Nick Hern Books published text. Describing it as 'divided into two acts' may mislead students who cite 'Act 2' as a dramatic reference in exams when the text uses 'Scene' numbering.
findings.correction: The play is organised in eight scenes. There is a discernible structural shift roughly in the middle — the first half establishing tension, the second half escalating into confrontation and resolution — but references in analysis should use scene numbers ('Scene 1', 'Scene 7') rather than 'Act 1'/'Act 2'.
findings.source: Oak National Academy lesson series has individual dedicated lessons for all 8 scenes (Scene 3, Scene 5, Scene 6, Scene 7, Scene 8 confirmed by lesson titles in search results); WJEC Eduqas PDF resource organises content by scene. Nick Hern Books published text uses scene divisions.

summary.critical_fabricated_plot_point: Across 10 lessons (5 AQA + 5 OCR), the content claims Enid left a child behind in Jamaica — this plot event does not occur in the published play. This single invented plot point ripples through character analysis, thematic analysis, and the resolution lesson, producing consistent misinformation about Enid's motivation and the play's emotional climax. It must be removed from all 10 lessons.
summary.critical_character_inversion: Across all 8 plot/character lessons (4 AQA + 4 OCR), Del and Viv's age order is inverted: the lessons call Viv the elder daughter and Del the younger. The play text gives Del as 18 (elder) and Viv as 17 (younger). This error compounds with the pregnancy misattribution — the lessons give Viv's pregnancy as a plot point, when it is Del who becomes pregnant.
summary.structural_note: The play is structured in 8 scenes, not two formal acts. Lessons should use scene numbers when referencing specific moments.
summary.accurate_elements: Context lessons (L1 AQA and OCR) are broadly accurate on Windrush history, the 1948 British Nationality Act, Empire Windrush, Brixton riots, Pinnock's theatrical significance, the 2018 Bush Theatre revival, and the play's thematic concerns. The Language lesson (L7) is accurate on code-switching, patois vs standard English, and character linguistic positions. The Themes lesson (L8) correctly identifies Belonging, Motherhood, Generational Divide, and Racism as major themes, though the abandoned-child fabrication distorts the Motherhood section.
summary.boards_affected: AQA (unit e92bde24) and OCR (unit 0319c0b5) — both boards share the same content_html for most lessons (L2–L7 are identical or near-identical between boards). Fixes applied to the AQA versions will resolve most OCR issues simultaneously.
